title: Geometry-Controlled Magnetic and Electronic Landscapes in Anisotropic van der Waals Materials
authors: Maciej Śmiertka, Ewelina Cybula, Oliwia Janikowska, Bartosz Hołyński, Gayatri, Grzegorz Krasucki, Mariusz Hasiak, Kseniia Mosina, Zdenek Sofer, Adam Babiński, Maciej R Molas, Paulina Plochocka, Michał Baranowski
abstract: Electronic structure in van der Waals materials is commonly engineered through composition, strain, electrostatic gating and heterostructure assembly. Here we introduce geometronics, a concept in which substrate geometry locally reorients an anisotropic crystal, transforming homogeneous external perturbation into programmable magnetic and electronic landscapes. We demonstrate this concept using a bilayer of the antiferromagnetic semiconductor CrSBr transferred onto an inverted pyramidal nanoindentation, where the local crystal orientation with respect to the external magnetic field drives the coexistence of antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic phases within a single continuous crystal. The resulting magnetic landscape creates a switchable excitonic potential well of up to 10--12 meV, directly visualised by spatially resolved spectroscopy. More generally, geometronics provides a universal route for deterministically programmed electronic and magnetic landscapes without modifying the material itself. It therefore establishes substrate topography as a new design principle that exploits the intrinsic anisotropy of layered van der Waals materials.
summary: This work introduces 'geotronics,' a method that uses substrate topography to locally reorient anisotropic van der Waals materials like CrSBr. By conforming the material to patterned substrates, the authors demonstrate that a uniform external field can create spatially varying magnetic and electronic landscapes. This establishes substrate geometry as a powerful, non-invasive design principle for creating tunable quantum functionalities.
main_problem: To achieve dynamic, on-demand, and position-dependent control over the electronic and magnetic structure of materials, moving beyond fixed properties set during fabrication.
main_result: The substrate topography can deterministically program local magnetic and electronic landscapes, creating switchable excitonic potential wells within a single, continuous crystal.
method: The study uses the concept of 'geotronics,' where the mechanical conformability of anisotropic van der Waals materials is exploited by transferring them onto substrates with controlled topography (e.g., nanoindentation pits).
model_or_system: The system studied is a bilayer of the antiferromagnetic semiconductor CrSBr. The key principle relies on the material's intrinsic anisotropy and mechanical compliance to the substrate geometry.
key_observables: Spatially resolved photoluminescence (PL) spectra, energy contrast ($\Delta E$) between flat and inclined regions, and local magnetic phase coexistence.
important_parameters: Local crystal tilt angle ($	heta \approx 10^\circ–20^\circ$), applied magnetic field ($B$), and the resulting excitonic energy contrast ($\sim 10–12 	ext{ meV}$).
main_assumptions: The approach assumes the material is mechanically compliant enough to conform to the substrate topography and that the electronic/magnetic response is highly sensitive to local crystal orientation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the concept of geometronics using nanoindentation pits, showing PL spectra maps and line scans that demonstrate the field-dependent energy contrast and localized modulation of the excitonic potential.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the concept of geometronics, demonstrates its feasibility using CrSBr on nanoindented substrates via PL spectroscopy, and concludes by establishing substrate topography as a universal design principle for programming electronic and magnetic functionalities.
why_interesting: The ability to program quantum properties (like excitonic potentials or magnetic order) using purely geometric control, rather than chemical doping or junction fabrication, offers a novel platform for realizing tunable quantum devices.
